title: log/slog: levels, attributes, handlers, JSON output
summary: log/slog (Go 1.21) logs a message plus typed key-value attributes; a Handler turns each record into text for people or JSON for machines. Loggers carry context with With, levels change at run time with a LevelVar.

examples.title: The same calls through TextHandler and JSONHandler

annotations.note: ReplaceAttr sees every attribute before it is written, including the built-in time, level and msg. Returning a zero Attr drops it. The same hook renames keys or masks personal data for a whole handler.
Before SetDefault, the top-level functions go through the old log package: stderr, its timestamp format, nothing in the compared output.

The call sites don't know the format; the Handler decides. Switching a service to JSON is a one-line change at startup. The Debug call produces nothing, because a handler's default minimum level is Info.

Alternating keys and values. TextHandler quotes a value only when it contains spaces, non-printing characters, quotes or "=", so İzmir stays bare and "Ayşe Yılmaz" is quoted. JSON keeps the UTF-8 as is, without \u escapes.

Typed constructors (slog.Duration, slog.Int) can't get out of step the way loose key-value pairs can. Group nests attributes: db.table in text, a nested object in JSON. A Duration is "1.5s" in text but nanoseconds (1500000000) in JSON.
An error value is written as its Error() string in both formats. Use a consistent key such as "err" so you can search for it.

examples.title: With, WithGroup, a LevelVar, and LogValuer for redaction

annotations.note: A type with a LogValue method decides its own log form, and the built-in handlers resolve it before writing. Token logs as REDACTED and User as its ID, without the e-mail, and no call site has to remember.
A LevelVar is a Leveler you can change while the program runs; its zero value is Info. HandlerOptions.Level also accepts a fixed level such as slog.LevelWarn.
With returns a new logger that adds request_id and method to every record. Pass reqLog down the request instead of repeating the IDs at each call.
The first Debug is dropped, the second appears: same code, level changed by level.Set with no restart.
WithGroup prefixes the keys of later attributes: payment.amount in text, a "payment" object in JSON. Attributes added earlier by With stay outside the group.
A key without a value compiles; the handler prints !BADKEY. go vet's slog check reports the call ("missing a final value").

examples.title: One logger, two audiences: NewMultiHandler (Go 1.26) and SetDefault

annotations.note: Each handler has its own minimum level and format. stdout stands in for a log collector here; a CLI whose stdout carries results sends all logs to stderr instead.

NewMultiHandler (Go 1.26) passes each record to every handler that is enabled for its level. Before 1.26 this took a small hand-written Handler. SetDefault makes the logger the target of slog.Info and friends.
Both records reach the JSON handler; only the warning reaches the text handler, which is the line in the stderr pane.
After SetDefault, log.Printf output becomes an Info record on the same handler, so old code joins the structured stream unchanged while you migrate it.

use_cases: Services: one JSON object per line on stdout, for a collector such as Loki, Elasticsearch or CloudWatch
Request-scoped loggers: logger.With("request_id", id) created in middleware and passed down
Raising verbosity in production for a while with a LevelVar, without a restart
Migrating a codebase from log.Printf gradually: SetDefault routes the old calls through the new handler
strengths: In the standard library since Go 1.21, so most programs need no logging dependency; in Java, java.util.logging, SLF4J and Log4j still compete
Call sites are format-agnostic: the Handler chooses text or JSON, and switching is one line at startup
Redaction lives on the type (LogValuer), not at hundreds of call sites
Logger.LogAttrs with typed attributes avoids allocations, so logging on hot paths stays cheap
weaknesses: Key-value arguments are ...any: a missing value compiles and prints !BADKEY; only go vet catches it
Arguments are evaluated before the level check: Debug("x", "dump", expensive()) pays for expensive() even when Debug is off
The built-in handlers ignore the context.Context: getting a request or trace ID from ctx into the output needs a small custom Handler
TextHandler joins group keys with dots without escaping, so a.b.c is ambiguous to a parser; use JSON when machines read the logs

pitfalls.title: Unpaired keys and values
pitfalls.detail: The variadic list is untyped. Run go vet, whose slog check catches it (the vet subset that go test runs does not include it), or use slog.String, slog.Int and friends.

pitfalls.title: Paying for disabled debug logs
pitfalls.detail: Arguments are computed before the handler checks the level. Wrap expensive values in a LogValuer, or guard the call with logger.Enabled(ctx, slog.LevelDebug).

pitfalls.title: Durations in JSON are nanoseconds
pitfalls.detail: slog.Duration becomes an integer in JSON (1500000000) but 1.5s in text. Pick a unit in the key (took_ms) or convert in ReplaceAttr so dashboards agree.

pitfalls.title: Secrets and personal data in logs
pitfalls.detail: Log an e-mail address once and it is in every backup of your log store. Give sensitive types a LogValue method, or mask keys in ReplaceAttr.

quiz.q: JSONHandler logs slog.Duration("took", 1500*time.Millisecond). What appears in the output?
quiz.why: A Duration is an int64 count of nanoseconds, and the JSON handler writes the number; TextHandler writes the String form.

quiz.q: logger.Info("login", "user") has a key without a value. What happens?
options: The record is logged with !BADKEY=user; go vet warns
quiz.why: The arguments are ...any, so the compiler accepts it. The handler marks the stray value, and vet's slog check reports the call.

quiz.q: Where does a type-wide rule like "never log the API token" belong?
options: In a LogValue method on the token type
In a comment above the struct
quiz.why: The built-in handlers resolve LogValuer values before writing, so the rule holds wherever the value is logged.

quiz.q: After slog.SetDefault(l), what happens to log.Printf calls?
options: They still print in the old format to stderr
They become Info records on l's handler
quiz.why: SetDefault also redirects the log package's default logger to l's Handler, at the level set by SetLogLoggerLevel (Info by default).

body:
## Concept

A structured log record is a level, a message and a list of typed attributes, not one
formatted string. `log/slog` (Go 1.21) separates the two halves: a `Logger` collects
records at call sites, and a `Handler` decides which records to keep and how to write
them. The standard library ships `TextHandler` (`key=value` lines for people) and
`JSONHandler` (one JSON object per line for machines). Because messages stay constant
and the variables become attributes, you can search for `msg="payment failed"` and
group by `err` instead of writing regular expressions over prose.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: `Logger` ≈ an SLF4J logger, `Handler` ≈ a Logback appender plus encoder,
  `With` ≈ MDC values, but explicit and passed as a value instead of thread-local.
- Python: `logging` with a JSON formatter and `extra={...}`; `logger.With` is closer to
  structlog's `bind`. Levels are numbers in both (slog: Debug -4, Info 0, Warn 4, Error 8).
- Node: very close to pino: one JSON object per line, child loggers (`pino.child`) ≈
  `With`, levels filtered before formatting.
- C/C++: no standard equivalent; spdlog-style sinks are the `Handler` idea.

## Design notes

Configure logging once in `main`: build the handler (JSON in production, text in a
terminal) with a `LevelVar` as its level, and pass the `*slog.Logger` to the
components that log, as a constructor parameter. `slog.SetDefault` is for the parts you
don't control, such as libraries still calling `log.Printf`. Request-scoped attributes
come from `With` in the HTTP middleware.

Keep messages constant and put variables in attributes. Choose key names once
(`err`, `user_id`, `request_id`) and stick to them: the log store indexes keys, not
your intentions. For a CLI, logs and diagnostics go to stderr so stdout stays clean for
results, as in the fmt lesson; for a service, the collector usually reads stdout.

expected.with-levels:
level=INFO msg=login request_id=r-42 method=POST user.id=7 token=REDACTED
level=DEBUG msg="cache lookup" request_id=r-42 method=POST hit=false
level=INFO msg=charged request_id=r-42 method=POST payment.amount=120 payment.currency=TRY
level=INFO msg="odd arguments" request_id=r-42 method=POST !BADKEY=user
